  | skglm 0.5                                     | Constant-Lipschitz CD | Gradient ($L_0 = 1/4$)                                      |
  | glmnet (`type.logistic = "modified.Newton"`)  | MM-IRLS               | Gradient ($L_0 = 1/4$) per outer iteration                  |
  | biglasso (`alg.logistic = "MM"`)              | MM-IRLS               | Gradient ($L_0 = 1/4$) per outer iteration                  |
  | glmnet (`type.logistic = "Newton"`)           | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | biglasso (`alg.logistic = "Newton"`, default) | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | adelie                                        | Local-IRLS            | Implicit, via weighted-centered-features parameterization   |
  | LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET, L1-LR)                  | Prox-Newton           | Convergence on the quadratic; intercept unregularized       |
  | BlitzL1                                       | Prox-Newton           | Combined-direction backtrack + post-step Newton convergence |

  : Classification of CD-based production solvers by algorithmic family and
    intercept update on the original loss. Local-IRLS and prox-Newton rows
    freeze the Hessian within each subproblem; BlitzL1 additionally applies a
    post-step 1-D Newton loop on the original loss. {#tbl-classification}

A consequence of the table is that two production solvers---LIBLINEAR
(newGLMNET) and BlitzL1---end up with the exact strategy on the intercept at the
boundary of each prox-Newton step. BlitzL1 arrives there by design, with an
explicit 1-D Newton convergence loop on the original loss after each subproblem;
LIBLINEAR arrives there as a byproduct of leaving the intercept unregularized
inside the inner CD, whose QP convergence carries the intercept to its
conditional minimum on the quadratic. The within-pass drift of
@eq-intercept-drift penalizes exact-strategy within direct CD because the inner
Hessian drifts between iterations; that critique does not apply at the
prox-Newton boundary, where the next subproblem's Hessian is recomputed anyway.
The structural distinction between the families thus carries over to a sensible
recommendation: use Newton on the intercept within direct CD, and run the exact
strategy at the linearization boundary inside IRLS or prox-Newton. The
production solvers that fit serious imbalanced-GLM problems in practice appear
to have arrived at exactly this prescription.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-irls-comparison
#| fig-cap: Direct CD and IRLS on an imbalanced logistic design. The panels show
#|   relative duality gap versus time for $\mu_0 = 0.99$, $n = 500$, $p = 1000$,
#|   $s = 10$, $\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$, and three random seeds. The
#|   Local-IRLS curve is shown once because the three intercept strategies
#|   coincide on the inner quadratic.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-irls-comparison.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-10)
df.it = "seed = " .* string.(df.it)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :it)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250)),
)
```

@fig-irls-comparison realizes both predictions empirically: MM-IRLS stalls on
the same plateau as Direct-CD with the gradient strategy under $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
while Local-IRLS converges on the same problem. The strategy collapse within
Local-IRLS is exact, not approximate: once $L_0^{\text{inner}} = H_{00}$, all
three strategies share the single inner update
$-\partial_0 \tilde F^{(t)} / H_{00}$ and so produce bit-identical iterates; the
figure therefore plots only one of them. The unit tests assert this directly:
the intercept and coefficient paths under the gradient, Newton, and exact
strategies agree exactly (`==`, not within a tolerance).

A reader may notice that Local-IRLS also outpaces Direct-CD with the Newton
strategy on this problem. This reflects the broader trade-off between
algorithmic families rather than a comparison of intercept strategies: IRLS-CD
enjoys a constant inner Hessian and locally quadratic outer convergence, which
favors it on canonical-link GLMs where the linearization is tight. Direct-CD has
the edge when $f'''$ is large (e.g.\
Poisson with extreme rates, where each linearization is loose far from the
current iterate), when working-response instability under saturation matters, or
when screening and working-set methods (standard in modern $\ell_1$ solvers)
compose poorly with re-linearization\ [@bertrand2022]. Our strategy analysis is
orthogonal to this family choice: within either family, the recommendation
against the gradient strategy and in favor of Newton carries through.

## Results {#sec-results}

This section tests the theory empirically, first on controlled simulations and
then on real data.

### Methodology and Reproducibility {#sec-methodology}

All internal-solver experiments use the `Intercepts` Julia package on Julia 1.11
with the default OpenBLAS. We report outer-pass counts as the primary work
metric: one pass is one sweep through all $p$ coordinates plus an intercept
update, and "passes to tolerance" means a relative duality gap of $10^{-8}$
unless noted. Pass budgets (`maxit`) are 1000 for the single-$\lambda$ figures
and 5000 for the heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg; cells that miss tolerance are
shown at the cap. Synthetic designs are standardized, use cyclic coordinate
ordering unless noted, and use AR(1) feature correlation $\rho = 0.6$ by
default. Seeds are fixed per script. The heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg averages
three seeds per cell; the other figures use one because the strategy effect
dominates seed-to-seed variation.

Real-data experiments use pinned datasets from Zenodo and standardize them
before fitting. The repository includes the code needed to retrieve these data
and to generate the shared standardized problem used in the production-solver
comparison. That comparison runs glmnet 4.1-10 (R), biglasso 1.6-1 (R), adelie
1.0-8 (R), skglm 0.5 (Python), LIBLINEAR through scikit-learn's
`solver="liblinear"` wrapper, and BlitzL1 at commit `aef8d02`. Given the cached
inputs, the drivers are otherwise deterministic, so each solver is run once per
tolerance setting while sweeping its native convergence parameter over a broad
range. The exact commands, tolerance grids, and iterate caps are documented with
the repository materials.

All experiment outputs are cached and ship with the repository. Most figures
therefore re-render from cache, so refreshing a panel means rerunning the code
that generated it; the illustrative @fig-parametric instead runs live at render
time as a small reproducible example. The Julia, R, and Python toolchains are
pinned in the repository and use their default OpenBLAS builds with no thread
pinning. Hardware: a single x86_64 Linux workstation with an AMD Ryzen 9 7900
(12 cores, 24 threads) and 64 GB of RAM; wall-clock numbers in this paper are
indicative rather than benchmark-grade. Source code and cached results ship with
the paper repository.

### Simulated Data

We begin with the simplest prediction from @sec-theory. The Schur-coupling
residual (@eq-grad-residual) says that the gradient strategy's effective
intercept step is the bare gradient step scaled by $H_{00}/L_0$. As imbalance
pushes $\mu_0$ toward one, $H_{00}$ shrinks while $L_0 = 1/4$ stays fixed, so
the intercept update should slow.

@fig-mu-extreme shows exactly that collapse on the standardized binary-logistic
design ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, $\rho = 0.6$,
$\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$) used throughout the simulated experiments below.
The gradient strategy is competitive at $\mu_0 = 0.5$, slows visibly past
$\mu_0 = 0.9$, and fails to reach the tolerance within budget at $\mu_0 = 0.99$.
By contrast, the Newton and exact strategies lie almost directly on top of each
other across the full sweep. That overlap is the outer-pass content of
@eq-intercept-drift; @sec-per-pass-cost returns to the per-pass inner work on
which those two strategies still differ. The gradient-versus-Newton scaling with
$\mu_0$ and $\lambda$ on the same design is taken up in @sec-imbalance-reg and
@fig-mu-reg-gradient.

### Real Data

The same scaling should appear on real problems, not just on the simulated
design. We therefore run the three strategies on six LIBSVM benchmark problems
at $\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$, listed in @tbl-real-logreg-problems and
ordered by the predicted slowdown $L_0/H_{00} = 1 / (4 \mu_0 (1 - \mu_0))$ (the
table lists its reciprocal $H_{00}/L_0$). The set spans a $9 \times$ range in
$L_0/H_{00}$ and five distinct design families: the Webb web-pages binary w1a, a
subsampled news20.binary bag-of-words text design (news20-3pct, 60 positives and
1\,940 negatives drawn deterministically from `news20.binary`), the UCI Adult
census (a4a) at moderate imbalance, the high-dimensional genomic leukemia
microarray ($n \ll p$, penalty-dominated), the small-$p$ Wisconsin breast cancer
panel, and dense balanced gisette.

The two most imbalanced problems, w1a and news20-3pct, are especially useful.
They sit at nearly the same $\mu_0$ on very different designs---a $300$-feature
sparse web indicator panel versus a $1.3\mathrm{M}$-vocabulary text
bag-of-words. Any prediction that survives both is therefore not a quirk of w1a
in particular.

  | dataset       | $n$   | $p$   | density | $\mu_0$ | $H_{00}/L_0$ |
  | :------------ | ----: | ----: | :------ | ------: | -----------: |
  | w1a           | 2,477 |   300 | sparse  |   0.029 |        0.113 |
  | news20-3pct   | 2,000 | 4,675 | sparse  |   0.030 |        0.116 |
  | a4a           | 4,781 |   123 | sparse  |   0.248 |        0.747 |
  | leukemia      |    38 | 7,129 | dense   |   0.711 |        0.823 |
  | breast-cancer |   683 |    10 | dense   |   0.350 |        0.910 |
  | gisette       | 6,000 | 5,000 | dense   |   0.500 |        1.000 |

  : LIBSVM problems used in @fig-real-logreg. $\mu_0$ is the positive-class
    marginal, and $H_{00}/L_0 = 4\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$. news20-3pct is a deterministic
    60/1\,940 subsample of `news20.binary`; after subsampling, features with
    fewer than 20 nonzeros are dropped. {#tbl-real-logreg-problems}

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-logreg
#| fig-cap: Real-data logistic convergence on six LIBSVM problems. The panels
#|   show relative duality gap versus time for the three intercept strategies at
#|   $\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$, in the problem order of
#|   @tbl-real-logreg-problems.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "real-logreg.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-10)
df.dataset = replace.(
    df.dataset,
    "gisette_scale" => "gisette",
    "news20-imb" => "news20-3pct",
)

dataset_order = ["w1a", "news20-3pct", "a4a", "leukemia", "breast-cancer", "gisette"]

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :time => "Time (s)",
        :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
        color = :strategy,
        layout = :dataset => sorter(dataset_order...),
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (900, 500)),
)
```

@fig-real-logreg confirms the prediction in both directions. The two
severe-imbalance points reproduce the simulated gradient slowdown on very
different sparse designs: w1a ($\mu_0 = 0.029$, a $300$-feature web indicator
panel) needs ${ \approx }5 \times$ more gradient passes than Newton to relative
gap $10^{-6}$, and news20-3pct ($\mu_0 = 0.030$, a $4\,675$-feature bag-of-words
text panel after dropping low-support vocabulary) reproduces a
${ \approx }6 \times$ ratio at $10^{-4}$ before hitting the $120\mathrm{s}$
wall-time cap. Both sit within the constant-factor offset of the leading-order
$L_0/H_{00}$ prediction that @fig-rate-gap exhibits, and the cross-design
agreement shows the gap is a property of the response imbalance, not of the w1a
design specifically. The mild-slowdown middle (a4a, breast-cancer) gives
gradient/Newton ratios between $1.3$ and $2.3$, consistent with their
$H_{00}/L_0 \in [0.75,0.91]$. The two predicted-benign cells are the framework's
negative controls: leukemia ($n \ll p$, penalty-dominated) and gisette (dense,
balanced, $\mu_0 = 0.5$, $H_{00}/L_0 = 1$) both have the three strategies
overlay each other. The exact strategy tracks bare Newton on every panel,
consistent with @eq-intercept-drift at this tolerance.

The Poisson family puts a sharper version of the same prediction on real data.
PoissonLoss has no global upper bound on $f''(\eta) = e^\eta$, so $L_0 = \infty$
and the gradient-strategy update degenerates: the per-pass change is
$-\sum_i (\hat\mu_i - y_i)/(L_0 n) = 0$, an exact no-op on the intercept. We
test this on the congress109 phrase-count corpus of @taddy2015distributed:
$n = 529$ speakers from the 107th--109th US Congress, $p = 999$ political
phrases (the 1\,000-phrase vocabulary with the response phrase removed). The
response $y_i$ is speaker $i$'s count of the phrase `american.people`
($\bar y = 11.83$, $y_{\max} = 396$), the highest-frequency phrase in the
corpus; the features are the remaining $999$ phrase counts after column
standardisation. This is the distributed-multinomial-regression construction of
@taddy2015distributed---a multinomial-over-vocabulary approximated by an
independent Poisson lasso per term---and the baseline rate $\bar y \approx 12$
puts the cold-start intercept overshoot $\bar y - 1 \approx 10.83$ versus the
exact $\log(\bar y) \approx 2.47$ in the regime where the synthetic cold-start
sweep in @fig-cold-start-poisson starts ($\mu_0 = 10$). Same
$\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$ convention as the logistic panel; cyclic CD with
a $1\,000$-pass budget.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-poisson
#| fig-cap: Poisson regression on congress109. The plot shows relative duality
#|   gap versus time for the four intercept strategies at $n = 529$, $p = 999$,
#|   $\bar y = 11.83$, and $\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "real-poisson.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])
df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-10)

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(:time => "Time (s)", :relgaps => "Relative duality gap", color = :strategy)
draw(visual(Lines) * spec, axis = (yscale = log10,), figure = (; size = (600, 380)))
```

The gradient-strategy collapse in @fig-real-poisson is the strongest empirical
form of the $L_0 = \infty$ structural-inadequacy claim from
@eq-grad-residual---no tuning, no problem-specific imbalance level, just the
loss family. The Newton-class strategies agree on a single trajectory because
the cdsolver's per-coordinate Armijo loop (Tseng--Yun sufficient decrease,
@algo-cd) absorbs the cold-start overshoot before the first intercept update
fires; the synthetic sweep of @fig-cold-start-poisson shows the same
coincidence, with the guarded and unguarded relative-gap curves staying inside
the seed-to-seed spread at every baseline rate we ran.

### Cyclic vs Permuted Ordering {#sec-ordering}

The within-pass drift argument of @eq-intercept-drift is agnostic to coordinate
ordering, but a residual concern is that strict cyclic order deterministically
pairs the intercept solve with the same first coordinate on every pass, which
could compound the drift. Under the per-coordinate Armijo backtrack that the
cdsolver applies after every coordinate update (@sec-methodology), this concern
does not materialize: on the w1a benchmark of @fig-first-example all three
strategies converge under both orderings and the pass-count differences are
within a factor of $1.4$ (@fig-first-example-ordering). Cyclic order is in fact
slightly faster than permuted on this problem for Newton ($157$ vs $187$ passes)
and for exact ($149$ vs $197$), with the gradient strategy at $\approx 840$
passes under either rule. The qualitative ranking of the three
strategies---Newton and exact fast, gradient slow---is the same under both, and
we use cyclic CD as the default elsewhere in the paper.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-first-example-ordering
#| fig-cap: Ordering comparison on w1a. The panels show relative duality gap
#|   versus time under cyclic (top) and permuted (bottom) coordinate ordering
#|   for the same configuration as @fig-first-example.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "first-example-ordering.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-10)

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :time => "Time (s)",
        :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
        color = :strategy,
        row = :ordering,
    )

draw(visual(Lines) * spec, axis = (; yscale = log10), figure = (; size = (500, 500)))
```

### Warm-Started Path {#sec-warmstart-path}

The single-$\lambda$ experiments above stress the strategies in their hardest
regime---cold start, large $|\partial_0 F|$ at iterate zero---which is also the
setting in which the theoretical critique of @eq-intercept-drift and the
imbalance collapse of @eq-grad-residual bite hardest. Production users rarely
solve a single $\lambda$ in isolation; they sweep a grid
$\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > \dots > \lambda_K$ and warm-start each subproblem from
the previous solution. As the warm-start argument above suggests, warm-starting
begins each subproblem with $|\partial_0 F|$ already small. The Newton-coupling
bias (@eq-newton-coupling) then predicts that the bare Newton step is
essentially exact at the start, so $k_0 \in \{1, 2\}$ in the exact strategy and
the $k_0 - 1$ per-pass overhead evaporates. The gradient-strategy collapse
should also soften because the iterate is close to optimum and the $H_{00}/L_0$
shrinkage acts on an already-small residual.

We test this by solving an $\ell_1$-logistic path on two problems---a simulated
standardized design ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, $\mu_0 = 0.9$,
$\rho = 0.6$) and the w1a benchmark used in @fig-first-example---over a
geometrically spaced grid of $K = 20$ values from $\lambda_{\max}$ down to
$5 \cdot 10^{-3}\lambda_{\max}$. Each subproblem is run to relative-gap
tolerance $10^{-8}$ or to a budget of 300 outer passes / 20 wall-seconds,
whichever comes first. We compare the three strategies, each under both warm
start (initialized from the previous-$\lambda$ solution) and cold start
(re-initialized at zero), and under both cyclic and permuted feature ordering.
The main-text panels show cyclic CD; @fig-warm-start-full and
@fig-warm-start-mechanism-full give the full grid over both orderings.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start
#| fig-cap: Warm-started and cold-started regularization paths. The panels show
#|   outer passes per subproblem along a logistic-regression $\lambda$ path
#|   under cyclic CD; dashed lines use warm starts, solid lines cold starts, and
#|   curves capped at 300 hit the pass budget. The left panel shows the
#|   simulated imbalanced problem ($\mu_0 = 0.9$) and the right panel w1a.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-warmstart-path.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(
    df,
    [
        :reg_grid,
        :passes,
        :times,
        :init_relgap,
        :final_relgap,
        :init_partial0F,
        :nnz_solution,
    ],
)

df.start_kind = ifelse.(df.warm_start, "warm", "cold")
df.ordering = ifelse.(df.randomize, "permuted", "cyclic")

# In-text slice: cyclic ordering only (the paper's default; @sec-ordering shows
# permuted differs by ≤1.4× and never changes the ranking). The full
# ordering × dataset grid is @fig-warm-start-full in the appendix.
df_cyclic = filter(:ordering => ==("cyclic"), df)

spec_passes = data(df_cyclic) *
    mapping(
        :reg_grid => L"$\lambda / \lambda_{\max}$",
        :passes => "Outer passes",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_passes,
    axis = (xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 320)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start-mechanism
#| fig-cap: Initial intercept gradients along the regularization path. The
#|   panels show $|\partial_0 F|$ at the initial iterate of each subproblem for
#|   the same path and cyclic-CD setup as @fig-warm-start; dashed lines use warm
#|   starts and solid lines cold starts.

spec_partial = data(df_cyclic) *
    mapping(
        :reg_grid => L"$\lambda / \lambda_{\max}$",
        :init_partial0F => L"$|\partial_0 F|$ at initialization",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_partial,
    axis = (xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 320)),
)
```

The mechanism panel (@fig-warm-start-mechanism) verifies the premise:
warm-starting drives $|\partial_0 F|$ toward zero as $\lambda$ shrinks and the
previous-$\lambda$ solution moves closer to the current optimum. Cold start, by
contrast, sets the initial iterate to zero at every $\lambda$, so
$|\partial_0 F|$ is the marginal class imbalance---roughly $10^2$ on the
simulated problem and $1.2 \times 10^3$ on w1a, identical across strategies.

The pass-count panel (@fig-warm-start) shows the expected compression, with one
caveat. On both problems and both orderings, warm-starting trims the few
pass-budget-capped subproblems for the Newton and exact strategies (on w1a from
$2$--$4$ out of $20$ cold to $2$ out of $20$ warm, depending on ordering and
strategy) and brings their curves nearly on top of each other. This is exactly
what @eq-intercept-drift suggests: once $|\partial_0 F|$ is already small, the
$k_0 - 1$ per-pass penalty of the exact strategy largely disappears.
Warm-starting also tightens the bare Newton solve at very small $\lambda$ on
w1a, where the cold-start trajectory hits the pass budget at relative gaps two
to three orders of magnitude looser than its warm-start counterpart.

The compression is uneven, however. The gradient strategy is essentially
unaffected by warm-starting on w1a---both cold and warm hit the pass budget on
$11$--$12$ of $20$ subproblems, with the curves overlaying. This is
@eq-grad-residual biting at every subproblem: the imbalance factor $H_{00}/L_0$
remains microscopic at the warm-start iterate, so even a near-optimal starting
point cannot compensate for the shrinking correction. The simulated problem
($\mu_0 = 0.9$) sits in the milder regime where all three strategies are
competitive cold, and warm-start contributes only a uniform $\approx 5\%$
reduction in pass count across the board.

Warm-starting therefore narrows the gap between the Newton-class strategies:
bare Newton and the exact strategy become hard to distinguish in practice. It
does not, however, rescue the gradient strategy. The recommendation from
@eq-intercept-drift still stands---bare Newton in direct CD, exact strategy at
the prox-Newton/IRLS boundary---with the added nuance that the exact strategy
becomes a defensible alternative when a path solve is already being used.

### Per-Pass Cost Decomposition {#sec-per-pass-cost}

The pass-count and wall-clock figures above conflate two distinct quantities
that the within-pass drift (@eq-intercept-drift) separates: the *number of outer
passes* needed to reach a tolerance and the *per-pass inner cost* paid at the
intercept update. The claim there is that the exact strategy pays $k_0 - 1$
extra inner Newton steps per outer pass with no commensurate rate improvement,
where $k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$ is the number of inner steps consumed
to drive $|\partial_0 F| < \varepsilon$ at the end of the pass via quadratic
Newton convergence on the 1D intercept subproblem. We instrument the solver to
record $k_0$ for every outer pass and compare the resulting cost trajectories
against the relative-gap trajectories on the imbalanced simulated design of
@fig-mu-extreme ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, cyclic CD,
$\lambda / \lambda_{\max} = 0.05$, tolerance $10^{-8}$), sweeping
$\mu_0 \in \{0.5,0.9,0.99\}$ to vary the cold-start magnitude of
$|\partial_0 F|$.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-per-pass-cost
#| fig-cap: Per-pass inner Newton work under the exact strategy. The panels show
#|   the number of intercept Newton steps $k_0$ versus outer-pass index for
#|   $\mu_0 \in \{0.5, 0.9, 0.99\}$ on the simulated design of @fig-mu-extreme.
#|   The dashed line at $k_0 = 1$ marks the Newton strategy.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-per-pass-cost.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:pass, :inner_steps, :cum_inner_steps, :relgap_after, :time])
df.μ0_label = [L"$\mu_0 = %$(v)$" for v in df.μ0]
df_exact = filter(:strategy => ==("exact"), df)

spec_cost = data(df_exact) *
    mapping(
        :pass => "Outer pass",
        :inner_steps => L"Inner Newton steps per pass ($k_0$)",
        col = :μ0_label,
    ) *
    visual(Lines)

spec_ref = mapping([1]) * visual(HLines, linestyle = :dash, color = :gray)

draw(spec_cost + spec_ref, facet = (; linkyaxes = :all), figure = (; size = (800, 260)))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-per-pass-progress
#| fig-cap: Per-pass progress on the same runs. The panels show relative duality
#|   gap after each outer pass for the Newton and exact strategies on the
#|   experiments of @fig-per-pass-cost.

spec_prog = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :pass => "Outer pass",
        :relgap_after => "Relative duality gap",
        color = :strategy,
        col = :μ0_label,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_prog,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkyaxes = :all),
    figure = (; size = (800, 260)),
)
```

The two figures make the $k_0 - 1$ overhead claim concrete. In
@fig-per-pass-cost, $k_0$ peaks on the cold-start pass (6, 4, and 3 inner steps
for $\mu_0 = 0.99, 0.9, 0.5$ respectively) and then decays to one as the iterate
approaches the joint optimum. Summed across the run, the relative
overhead---total inner Newton steps for the exact strategy divided by the Newton
strategy's pass-count baseline---is $1.30 \times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.5$,
$1.50 \times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.9$, and $1.59 \times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.99$. The trend
is monotone in the same imbalance that drives $|\partial_0 F|$ at cold start.

@fig-per-pass-progress shows why that extra work is hard to justify. The Newton
and exact strategies trace almost the same relative-gap curve and finish in
comparable pass counts (Newton: 109/107/121; exact: 109/108/120). In other
words, the exact strategy spends strictly more inner Newton work for essentially
the same outer-pass progress.

The penalty is modest because quadratic Newton convergence on the 1D intercept
subproblem keeps $k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$, well below the inner-loop
cap of 20, and most passes need only a single inner step. Still, the pattern is
clear: the exact strategy pays its price in the first few cold-start passes,
when $|\partial_0 F|$ is largest. The warm-start regime of @sec-warmstart-path
largely avoids that window.

### Imbalance and Regularization {#sec-imbalance-reg}

The single-$\lambda$ experiments above test the framework along one axis at a
time. The quantitative prediction of @eq-rate-gap is two-dimensional: the
gradient/Newton pass-count ratio scales with $L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$, and both
$\lambda$ and $\mu_0$ shift $\hat\eta$ and therefore $H_{00}$. We sweep
$\mu_0 \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99\}$ against
$\lambda/\lambda_{\max} \in \{0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01\}$ on the
standardized binary-logistic design of @fig-mu-extreme (3 seeds per cell),
running each strategy to a relative-gap tolerance of $10^{-8}$ or a budget of
5000 outer passes. We report pass counts rather than wall-clock to decouple the
per-coordinate Lipschitz-mismatch prediction from BLAS and memory effects.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-reg-gradient
#| fig-cap: Gradient-to-Newton pass-count ratios over the $(\mu_0,
#|   \lambda/\lambda_{\max})$ grid. The heatmap shows
#|   $\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{gradient}} / T_{\mathrm{Newton}})$ averaged over
#|   three seeds on the standardized logistic design; clipped cells mark runs
#|   that hit the 5000-pass budget.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-mu-reg-heatmap.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])

agg = combine(groupby(df, [:μ0, :reg, :strategy]), :passes => mean => :passes)

wide = unstack(agg, [:μ0, :reg], :strategy, :passes)
wide.gradient_ratio = wide.gradient ./ wide.newton
wide.exact_ratio = wide.exact ./ wide.newton
wide.reg_str = string.(wide.reg)
wide.μ0_str = string.(wide.μ0)

spec_grad = data(wide) *
    mapping(
        :reg_str =>
            sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") =>
            L"$\lambda / \lambda_{\max}$",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => L"$\mu_0$",
        :gradient_ratio => log10 => L"$\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{grad}}/T_{\mathrm{Newton}})$",
    )

draw(spec_grad * visual(Heatmap), figure = (; size = (560, 320)))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-reg-exact
#| fig-cap: Exact-to-Newton pass-count ratios over the $(\mu_0,
#|   \lambda/\lambda_{\max})$ grid. The heatmap shows
#|   $\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{exact}} / T_{\mathrm{Newton}})$ on the same grid and
#|   seed average as @fig-mu-reg-gradient, using a centered diverging colormap
#|   with range $\pm 0.1$.

spec_exact = data(wide) *
    mapping(
        :reg_str =>
            sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") =>
            L"$\lambda / \lambda_{\max}$",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => L"$\mu_0$",
        :exact_ratio =>
            log10 =>
            L"$\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{exact}}/T_{\mathrm{Newton}})$, range $\pm 0.1$",
    )

draw(
    spec_exact * visual(Heatmap),
    scales(Color = (; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = (-0.1, 0.1))),
    figure = (; size = (560, 320)),
)
```

The main pattern in @fig-mu-reg-gradient is simple: at any fixed $\lambda$,
greater imbalance makes the gradient strategy slower relative to Newton. The
gradient/Newton pass-count ratio rises from roughly one at $\mu_0 = 0.5$ to
about seven at $\mu_0 = 0.99$ for $\lambda \in \{0.05, 0.02\}\lambda_{\max}$,
the largest ratios on the grid. The $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
$\lambda = 0.01\lambda_{\max}$ corner is the only cell in which any run
saturates the 5000-pass budget, and it saturates for both strategies, so its
displayed ratio of $2.0$ reads as uninformative rather than extreme; we return
to it below.

At $\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$, the regime most relevant to the production
path experiments, the empirical ratios across the five $\mu_0$ values are
$\{1.0, 1.1, 1.8, 3.0, 6.8\}$. The corresponding iterate-level
$L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$ values at the Newton-converged solution are
$\{3.2, 3.3, 4.4, 5.7, 12.3\}$ (mean over three seeds). The theory therefore
gets the ordering and the growth right, but it overstates the magnitude by a
fairly stable factor: about $3 \times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.5$ and about $2 \times$ at
$\mu_0 = 0.99$. The cold-start proxy
$L_0/H_{00}(0) = 1/(4\mu_0(1 - \mu_0)) = \{1.00, 1.19, 2.78, 5.26, 25.25\}$ is
looser still at high imbalance because active features pull $H_{00}$ above its
intercept-only value $\mu_0(1 - \mu_0)$ at this $\lambda$. As $\lambda$ shrinks,
the active set widens, $H_{00}$ falls toward and beyond $\mu_0(1 - \mu_0)$, and
the empirical ratio grows with it. At $\lambda = 0.01\lambda_{\max}$, for
example, the empirical row for $\mu_0 \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95\}$ is
$\{1.7, 1.8, 4.0, 5.4\}$; we omit the $\mu_0 = 0.99$ corner because both Newton
and gradient hit the 5000-pass budget there, making the ratio uninformative.

By contrast, @fig-mu-reg-exact stays nearly flat at zero: the exact/Newton ratio
is approximately one across the plane, and no cell departs from unity by more
than $7\%$. This is the outer-pass content of @eq-intercept-drift. When both
methods converge, the exact strategy needs essentially the same number of outer
passes as bare Newton. Its price is therefore an inner-step overhead, not an
outer-pass overhead, which is exactly what @sec-per-pass-cost measures.

Taken together, the two heatmaps show what @eq-rate-gap does and does not
predict. Along the $H_{00}/L_0$ axis, it captures scaling and monotonicity well:
the empirical ratio grows as the intercept channel degrades
($H_{00}/L_0 \to 0$), and it rises monotonically with $\mu_0$ and with
$1/\lambda$. It does not predict the magnitude tightly. Across this grid the
empirical ratio sits about two to four times below the iterate-level
@eq-rate-gap prediction, which is what one would expect from a comparison built
from upper bounds and heuristic substitutions rather than from a sharp
iteration-complexity formula.

The centering sweep of @fig-rho-centering is where the agreement is weakest.
There, the empirical ratio does increase with $\bar\rho^2$, as @eq-rate-gap
requires, but it saturates at $L_0/H_{00}$ by $\bar\rho^2 \approx 0.04$ and then
stays there while the leading-order factor continues up to $\bar\rho^2 = 0.51$.
On that axis the theory gets the direction right, but not the shape or the
scale.

### Production Solvers {#sec-production-solvers}

Here we test the strategy-class predictions on six production solvers and three
imbalanced logistic problems: the shared synthetic design, w1a, and news20-3pct.
Together they cover both directions of imbalance and three data regimes ($p > n$
dense Gaussian, $n > p$ sparse binary, $n < p$ sparse text). Each problem fixes
$\lambda = 0.05 \cdot \lambda_{\max}$. All solvers run in their recommended path
mode (warm-start from $\lambda_{\max}$ down to $\lambda$ in 50 geometric
steps);[^cold-start-footnote] for each solver we sweep its convergence tolerance
and plot suboptimality against the work it exposes (CD passes, outer iterations,
or wall-clock time). The reference primal $F^\star$ is the minimum primal that
solver attains on that problem.

[^cold-start-footnote]: At single $\lambda$ without warm-starting, biglasso
    `alg.logistic = "Newton"` and adelie exhibit the unguarded-Newton cold-start
    failure of @eq-newton-coupling on the two extreme-imbalance real datasets
    used here; @sec-cold-start-diag reports the diagnostic.

We sort these solvers into two buckets by the intercept update each realizes on
the original loss\ (@tbl-classification). Bucket A contains the
gradient-strategy solvers---glmnet `modified.Newton`, biglasso `MM`, and
skglm---while Bucket B contains the local-IRLS solvers---glmnet `Newton`,
biglasso `Newton`, and adelie. LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1 sit outside the split
because their prox-Newton boundary effectively realizes the exact strategy. The
figure sequence follows that structure: within-package toggles in glmnet and
biglasso isolate the weight scheme, skglm 0.5 shows the direct-CD gradient case,
@fig-skglm-controlled isolates skglm's upstream Newton fix, and the
LIBLINEAR/BlitzL1 and adelie panels check the fast-converging side of the
prediction.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-glmnet
#| fig-cap: glmnet mode comparison on three imbalanced logistic problems. The
#|   panels show primal suboptimality versus inner CD passes for `type.logistic
#|   = "Newton"` and `"modified.Newton"` in path mode on the shared synthetic
#|   problem, w1a, and news20-3pct.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "glmnet.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "glmnet.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(
        @projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "glmnet.csv"),
    )),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,
)
df.mode = df.type

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :npasses,
        :subopt,
        color = :mode,
        col = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, xlabel = "Inner CD passes", ylabel = "Primal suboptimality"),
    figure = (; size = (800, 300)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-biglasso
#| fig-cap: biglasso mode comparison on three imbalanced logistic problems. The
#|   panels show primal suboptimality versus inner CD passes for `alg.logistic =
#|   "Newton"` and `"MM"` in path mode on the same three problems as
#|   @fig-real-glmnet.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "biglasso.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "biglasso.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(
        @projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "biglasso.csv"),
    )),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,

df.mode = df.alg

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :npasses,
        :subopt,
        color = :mode,
        col = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, xlabel = "Inner CD passes", ylabel = "Primal suboptimality"),
    figure = (; size = (800, 300)),

```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-skglm
#| fig-cap: skglm 0.5 on three imbalanced logistic problems. The panels show
#|   primal suboptimality versus `AndersonCD` outer iterations on the same three
#|   problems as @fig-real-glmnet.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(
        @projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "skglm.csv"),
    )),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,
)
df = df[df.n_iter .> 0, :]
sort!(df, [:problem, :n_iter])

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(:n_iter, :subopt, col = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"))
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        # xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "AndersonCD outer iterations",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (700, 300)),
)
```

These three panels establish the production-solver split cleanly. In glmnet and
biglasso, the within-package weight toggle produces exactly the slowdown one
would expect from the constant-majorant update. In skglm 0.5---the only
production solver in our survey whose intercept update is unambiguously the
gradient strategy---the trajectory has the same slow ramp predicted by the
Newton-coupling bias (@eq-newton-coupling) and the Schur-coupling residual
(@eq-grad-residual). That diagnosis motivated a pull request to skglm replacing
the gradient update with a Newton step; the change was merged upstream as commit
`8f9cbd77`.[^skglm-pr]

[^skglm-pr]: <https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/skglm/pull/337>, merged
    2026-05-13. skglm 0.6 is unreleased at the time of writing; the controlled
    comparison below pins the two relevant commits directly.

@fig-real-glmnet through @fig-real-skglm also make the high-level pattern easy
to read on fixed problems: the gradient-class solvers are slow, and the
Newton-class solvers are fast. To separate that claim from any other codebase
differences, @fig-skglm-controlled compares two skglm commits that differ only
in the intercept update: `b03644fe`, the last pre-fix commit and behaviorally
identical to the released 0.5, and `8f9cbd77`, the merged Newton fix. Running
the same `AndersonCD` driver on both yields a clean 30-cell comparison that
reproduces the trend of @fig-mu-reg-gradient---the ratio grows with $\mu_0$ and
with $1/\lambda$---at a far larger scale, and without the monotonicity holding
cell by cell. The pre-fix commit needs $30 \times$ the iterations of the
post-fix one already at $\mu_0 = 0.5$, $\lambda = 0.5\lambda_{\max}$, and up to
$417 \times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.99$, $\lambda = 0.01\lambda_{\max}$. The floor is
this high because `AndersonCD` reaches its tolerance in $1$ to $18$ outer
iterations once the intercept takes a Newton step, so any residual intercept
climb dominates the count; the $20$ of $90$ pre-fix runs that hit the
5000-iteration cap put a lower bound on their cell's ratio rather than a value.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-skglm-controlled
#| fig-cap: Within-skglm commit comparison. The heatmap shows
#|   $\log_{10}(T_{\mathtt{b03644fe}} / T_{\mathtt{8f9cbd77}})$ for `AndersonCD`
#|   across the same $(\mu_0,\lambda/\lambda_{\max})$ grid as
#|   @fig-mu-reg-gradient, averaged over three seeds; clipped cells mark runs
#|   that hit the 5000-iteration cap.

df_sk = DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "skglm-controlled", "results.csv")))
df_sk.strategy = ifelse.(df_sk.commit .== "b03644fe", "gradient", "newton")

agg_sk = combine(groupby(df_sk, [:mu0, :reg, :strategy]), :n_iter => mean => :n_iter)
wide_sk = unstack(agg_sk, [:mu0, :reg], :strategy, :n_iter)
wide_sk.skglm_ratio = wide_sk.gradient ./ wide_sk.newton
wide_sk.reg_str = string.(wide_sk.reg)
wide_sk.μ0_str = string.(wide_sk.mu0)

spec_sk = data(wide_sk) *
    mapping(
        :reg_str =>
            sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") =>
            L"$\lambda / \lambda_{\max}$",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => L"$\mu_0$",
        :skglm_ratio => log10 => L"$\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{pre}}/T_{\mathrm{post}})$",
    )

draw(spec_sk * visual(Heatmap), figure = (; size = (560, 320)))
```

The prox-Newton solvers tell the complementary story. If a solver realizes the
exact strategy at a prox-Newton boundary, it should converge quickly on these
problems. LIBLINEAR\ (newGLMNET) and BlitzL1 are the two production solvers in
our survey that fit this description. @fig-real-proxnewton reports their
wall-clock cost to reach $F^\star$ across the same three problems used above,
complementing the inner-pass curves for skglm 0.5 (gradient strategy on the
intercept) and glmnet's `modified.Newton` (the constant-majorant alternative).

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-proxnewton
#| fig-cap: Prox-Newton solvers on three imbalanced logistic problems. The
#|   panels show primal suboptimality versus wall-clock time for LIBLINEAR and
#|   BlitzL1 on the same three problems as @fig-real-glmnet. LIBLINEAR runs that
#|   hit its internal `max_iter` cap without further progress are omitted.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "proxnewton.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "proxnewton.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(
        @projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "proxnewton.csv"),
    )),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,
)
df = df[.!(df.solver .== "LIBLINEAR" .&& df.n_iter .>= 5000), :]
sort!(df, [:problem, :solver, :runtime])

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :runtime,
        :subopt,
        color = :solver,
        col = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, xlabel = "Time (s)", ylabel = "Primal suboptimality"),
    figure = (; size = (800, 300)),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = false),
)
```

adelie provides an independent confirmation from a different codebase. It builds
the same weighted Gaussian surrogate as glmnet `Newton`, but it realizes the
intercept implicitly: rather than updating $\beta_0$ as a coordinate inside the
inner CD pass, it weighted-centers the features at the start of each surrogate
and tracks the residual mean, reconstructing
$\beta_0 = \bar{y} + \overline{\mathrm{resid}}$ at the end of the inner solve.
By construction, the intercept therefore sits at the surrogate optimum on every
outer pass, with no separate update step.

That places adelie in the same class as glmnet `Newton` and biglasso `Newton`,
and @fig-real-adelie reports its per-tolerance wall-clock cost across the same
three problems used above. adelie's outer-IRLS criterion is coarser than
glmnet's coefficient-based `thresh`, which is reflected in a higher achievable
suboptimality from a single tolerance sweep. The quantity that matters for the
present argument, however, is per-iteration cost, and on that margin adelie sits
in the same range as the other local-IRLS solvers.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-adelie
#| fig-cap: adelie on three imbalanced logistic problems. The panels show primal
#|   suboptimality versus convergence tolerance on the same three problems as
#|   @fig-real-glmnet. The horizontal axis is the coupled outer/inner tolerance
#|   (`tol = irls_tol`).

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "adelie.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "adelie.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(
        @projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "adelie.csv"),
    )),
)
df_ref = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(
        @projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "skglm.csv"),
    )),
)
F_star = combine(groupby(df_ref, :problem), :primal => minimum => :F_star)
df = leftjoin(df, F_star, on = :problem)
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- df.F_star, 1.0e-15)
sort!(df, [:problem, :tol])

spec = data(df) *
    mapping(:tol, :subopt, col = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"))
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xreversed = true,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Convergence tolerance (tol = irls_tol)",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (800, 300)),
)
```

#### Poisson Family

The Poisson family separates the production solvers structurally before any
trajectory is recorded. PoissonLoss has $f''(\eta) = e^\eta$ unbounded on
$\mathbb{R}$, so no global Lipschitz upper bound exists; consequently neither
the $w \equiv 1/4$ MM majorant of glmnet `modified.Newton` and biglasso `MM` nor
the constant-Lipschitz coordinate step of skglm `AndersonCD` has a Poisson
analog. The status of each solver on this family is structural, not empirical:

- **glmnet** supports `family = "poisson"` with a single fitting mode
  (local-IRLS); no `type.poisson` switch exists.
- **biglasso** does not implement `family = "poisson"` at all; its signature is
  restricted to `gaussian`, `binomial`, `cox`, and `mgaussian`.
- **skglm** `AndersonCD` requires `datafit.get_lipschitz()`, which the `Poisson`
  datafit declines to implement
  (`AttributeError: Poisson is not   compatible with solver AndersonCD`). The
  gradient-class entry vanishes at the attribute-resolution layer.
- **skglm** `ProxNewton` pairs with the `Poisson` datafit through local
  prox-Newton subproblems and is the prox-Newton representative in the panel.
- **adelie** supports `glm.poisson(y)` through the same direct-Newton /
  weighted-centered-features parameterization as the logistic case.

Three Newton-class solvers therefore remain: glmnet, adelie, and skglm
`ProxNewton`. We run each in path mode on congress109 with
$\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$, sweeping the solver-specific tolerance.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-poisson-production
#| fig-cap: Production Poisson solvers on congress109. The plot shows primal
#|   suboptimality versus wall-clock time for glmnet, adelie, and skglm
#|   `ProxNewton` in path mode at $n = 529$, $p = 999$, $\bar y = 11.83$, and
#|   $\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$. $F^\star$ is the minimum primal observed
#|   across solvers and tolerances.

probdir = @projectroot("results", "real-solvers-poisson", "congress109")
df_gl = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(probdir, "glmnet.csv")))
df_ad = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(probdir, "adelie.csv")))
df_pn = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(probdir, "proxnewton.csv")))

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(solver = "glmnet", runtime = df_gl.runtime, primal = df_gl.primal),
    DataFrame(solver = "adelie", runtime = df_ad.runtime, primal = df_ad.primal),
    DataFrame(solver = "skglm ProxNewton", runtime = df_pn.runtime, primal = df_pn.primal),
)
F_star = minimum(df.primal)
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- F_star, 1.0e-15)
sort!(df, [:solver, :runtime])

spec = data(df) * mapping(:runtime, :subopt, color = :solver)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    legend = (; titlevisible = false),
    axis = (yscale = log10, xlabel = "Time (s)", ylabel = "Primal suboptimality"),
    figure = (; size = (500, 280)),
)
```

The Poisson panel therefore makes a structural point rather than an empirical
one. The within-package weight-scheme toggle that drives @fig-real-glmnet and
@fig-real-biglasso has no analog here, not because the package authors omitted
it, but because the loss family itself does not admit the $w \equiv 1/4$
surrogate that powers the gradient-class entries. Every working production
Poisson solver in our survey therefore lands on the Newton-class side of the
split, directly reflecting the framework's recommendation at the source-code
level.

#### Single-Lambda Cold Start {#sec-cold-start-diag}

The path-mode protocol used above warm-starts the inner CD past the cold-start
transient at $\beta = 0$. If we remove that ramp and solve a single $\lambda$
from scratch, the unguarded Newton intercept update predicted to be unstable by
@eq-newton-coupling does fail in production code on the two most imbalanced real
problems. The diagnostic in @tbl-cold-start-diag runs each solver at
$\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$ with $\text{eps} = 10^{-1}$, sweeping the iterate
cap from $10^1$ to $10^5$; the path-mode reference primal is $0.0634$ on w1a and
$0.0497$ on news20-3pct.

  | dataset     | solver                             | $\beta_0$                     | primal  | iterations             |
  | :---------- | :--------------------------------- | :---------------------------- | ------: | :--------------------- |
  | w1a         | biglasso `alg.logistic = "Newton"` | $-723$ (range $[-1722,-291]$) | $16.19$ | $10^5$ cap, oscillates |
  | w1a         | biglasso `alg.logistic = "MM"`     | $-3.51$                       | $0.088$ | $2$                    |
  | w1a         | adelie                             | ---                           |     --- | empty state returned   |
  | news20-3pct | biglasso `alg.logistic = "Newton"` | $-3.48$                       | $0.310$ | $2$ (premature stop)   |
  | news20-3pct | biglasso `alg.logistic = "MM"`     | $-3.48$                       | $0.089$ | $2$                    |
  | news20-3pct | adelie                             | $-5.22$                       | $0.052$ | converges              |

  : Single-$\lambda$ cold-start diagnostic on w1a and news20-3pct. Each row
    reports the intercept estimate, primal objective, and iteration count at
    $\lambda = 0.05\lambda_{\max}$ with $\text{eps} = 10^{-1}$; the iterate cap
    is swept from $10^1$ to $10^5$, and the path-mode reference primal is
    $0.0634$ on w1a and $0.0497$ on news20-3pct. {#tbl-cold-start-diag}

The main lesson of @tbl-cold-start-diag is that the global majorant $L_0 = 1/4$
acts as an $X$-free safeguard on the intercept: two scalars ($n$ and $\bar y$)
determine the step, and that is enough to absorb the cold-start transient at
trivial cost on the unpenalized coordinate. The analogous safeguard for a
coefficient would require column-norm information.

This matters in practice because unguarded Newton is the default in biglasso and
the only mode in adelie. On a benchmark like w1a, a user who omits path mode can
therefore receive no solution at all. The difference between w1a and
news20-3pct, despite their matched $\bar y$, shows that the failure is not
driven by the cold-start gradient magnitude alone. What matters is the IRLS
weight collapse after the first inner solve. On news20-3pct's wider sparse
design, the $\ell_1$ penalty pulls many entries to zero before the linear
predictor reaches extreme values, which dampens the cycle.

## Discussion

Across both theory and experiments, the intercept update turns out to be a
load-bearing choice rather than a minor implementation detail. For direct
coordinate descent on a smooth GLM loss, the best default is a Newton block step
with Armijo backtracking. It is insensitive to imbalance, needs no tuning, and
matches the exact strategy on outer-pass count without paying the $k_0 - 1$
extra inner Newton steps that the exact strategy spends each pass. The main
exception is the warm-started path setting of @sec-warmstart-path, where
$|\partial_0 F|$ is already small and the exact strategy's extra inner work
mostly disappears.

The guard should be part of that default, not treated as a loss-family-specific
option. On bounded-Hessian losses it is effectively free. On unbounded-Hessian
losses such as Poisson, it prevents the cold-start overshoot seen in
@fig-cold-start-poisson. The gradient strategy fails for the same reason it
fails under imbalance more generally: once $H_{00}/L_0$ becomes small---or once
$L_0 = \infty$ in Poisson---it stops making a meaningful intercept correction.

The production-solver survey turns this into a practical diagnostic. Solvers
that realize Newton-class behavior on the intercept---glmnet `Newton`, biglasso
`Newton`, adelie, LIBLINEAR, and BlitzL1---remain fast on the imbalanced
problems we study. Solvers that realize the gradient-class update---glmnet
`modified.Newton`, biglasso `MM`, and skglm 0.5---inherit the same imbalance
sensitivity as the direct-CD gradient strategy. The within-package toggles in
glmnet and biglasso, the before-and-after skglm comparison, and the structural
absence of gradient-class Poisson solvers all support that reading.

Multinomial problems make the issue more common rather than less. Every rare
class creates its own slow intercept direction, so long-tailed label
distributions naturally fall into the regime where gradient updates stall
(@fig-multinomial-imbalance, @fig-multinomial-sweep). The same block structure
also makes Newton and exact nearly indistinguishable there.

Our analysis has two main limitations. First, the Newton-strategy results are
*local*. @eq-newton-error and @eq-newton-coupling are Taylor identities for a
single Newton step, not a global convergence proof for CD with a Newton-updated
intercept, and the empirical evidence in @sec-results is supportive rather than
conclusive. A sharper rate analysis under restricted strong convexity would let
@eq-rate-gap predict the empirical pass-count constant, not just its scaling and
monotonicity (@sec-imbalance-reg).

Second, the production-solver experiments in @sec-production-solvers run on a
single shared problem. The heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg replicates the binary
direct-CD predictions across a 30-cell grid, but the cross-package comparison
does not yet sweep the full $(\mu_0, \lambda)$ plane. Extending the
production-solver sweep along those axes, and checking the multinomial
predictions against glmnet's symmetric-multinomial path and adelie's
multi-response solver, are natural next steps.

# Supplementary Figures {.unnumbered}

These are the full versions of the dense grids that the main text shows as
representative slices: the complete multinomial sweep
(@fig-multinomial-sweep-full, sliced to its four corners in
@fig-multinomial-sweep) and the warm-started-path grids over both coordinate
orderings (@fig-warm-start-full and @fig-warm-start-mechanism-full, shown for
cyclic CD only in @fig-warm-start and @fig-warm-start-mechanism).

```{julia}
#| label: fig-multinomial-sweep-full
#| fig-cap: Full multinomial imbalance-amplitude sweep. The panels show relative
#|   primal suboptimality versus outer-pass index over the full $4 \times 4$
#|   grid of rarest-class marginal $\bar p_K$ and feature amplitude from
#|   @fig-multinomial-sweep.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-multinomial-imbalance-sweep.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals, :pass])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-10)

agg = combine(
    groupby(df, [:p_K, :amplitude, :strategy, :pass]),
    :relgaps => median => :relgaps,
)

agg.p_K_str = [L"$\bar{p}_K = %$(v)$" for v in agg.p_K]
agg.amp_str = "amp = " .* string.(agg.amplitude)

spec = data(agg) *
    mapping(
        :pass => "Pass",
        :relgaps => "Relative primal suboptimality",
        color = :strategy,
        row = :p_K_str => sorter(
            L"$\bar{p}_K = 0.05$",
            L"$\bar{p}_K = 0.02$",
            L"$\bar{p}_K = 0.01$",
            L"$\bar{p}_K = 0.005$",
        ),
        col = :amp_str => sorter("amp = 0.5", "amp = 1.0", "amp = 1.5", "amp = 2.0"),
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 600)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start-full
#| fig-cap: Full warm-started and cold-started regularization paths. The panels
#|   show outer passes per subproblem along the logistic-regression $\lambda$
#|   path for cyclic CD (top) and permuted CD (bottom); dashed lines use warm
#|   starts, solid lines cold starts, and curves capped at 300 hit the pass
#|   budget.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-warmstart-path.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(
    df,
    [
        :reg_grid,
        :passes,
        :times,
        :init_relgap,
        :final_relgap,
        :init_partial0F,
        :nnz_solution,
    ],
)

df.start_kind = ifelse.(df.warm_start, "warm", "cold")
df.ordering = ifelse.(df.randomize, "permuted", "cyclic")

spec_passes = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :reg_grid => L"$\lambda / \lambda_{\max}$",
        :passes => "Outer passes",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
        row = :ordering,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_passes,
    axis = (; xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 500)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start-mechanism-full
#| fig-cap: Full initial-gradient regularization paths. The panels show
#|   $|\partial_0 F|$ at the initial iterate of each subproblem along the
#|   $\lambda$ path for cyclic CD (top) and permuted CD (bottom); dashed lines
#|   use warm starts and solid lines cold starts.

spec_partial = data(df) *
    mapping(
        :reg_grid => L"$\lambda / \lambda_{\max}$",
        :init_partial0F => L"$|\partial_0 F|$ at initialization",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
        row = :ordering,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_partial,
    axis = (; xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 500)),
)
```
